title: A Small Coin for the Truth

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 5. Today's news: the alley went back for noodles.*

The sheets hung all night, stiff and pale, waiting for the cold to pass. At dawn, Haru and Kichi carried them in a woven basket to the canal end. The air tasted of frost and fish.

Haru opened her mouth to call out the news. Her voice came out thin, like a mouse squeak behind a door. She tried again. Nothing.

Kichi, who had eaten three rice cakes on the way, took a sheet and rolled it into a horn. "News! News! The noodles are clean! The rumor is a lie!"

A woman stopped, clutching her straw hat. "Is it true?"

"I saw it with my own eyes," Haru said, loud and steady this time.

Kichi added, "It’s a real story. No foxes, no ghosts, just flour and water. Better than a rumor, and half the price."

The woman laughed, a bright, startled sound. She pulled a small coin from her apron. "I’ll take two. One for me, one for my sister-in-law who believes everything."

Haru smiled, her cheeks hot. The truth had a voice, and it was Kichi’s.
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron with a vermilion cord in her topknot, stands beside Kichi, a gangly boy in a moss-green coat and checked head towel, holding a rolled paper sheet near a canal, while a woman in a quilted coat smiles and offers a coin.

pages.text:
Bunta, the big seller with the deep straw hat, stopped mid-step. He did not buy a copy. He took one from the basket, unrolled it, and began to read.

"The Owl Alley Sheet," he boomed, his voice rolling over the packed earth of the alley. "The claim: Okiku’s noodles are made with sawdust. The proof: none. The truth: pure buckwheat, wheat and water, witnessed by a girl with ink-stained fingers."

He looked up. "I have sold many sheets. This one is quiet. But it is right. I will not charge you. Read it yourselves."

Gohei, thin and watchful, kept his eyes on the alley mouth, checking for officials. But the crowd did not move. They stood still, listening to the words hang in the cold air. For a moment, the noise of the street faded, and only the sound of Bunta’s voice remained, steady and clear.

Haru watched the people’s faces. They were not laughing. They were thinking. The truth had landed, and it stayed.
pages.image: Bunta, a large man in an indigo-striped kimono and a deep straw hat, stands in a narrow alley holding a paper sheet, his mouth open as he reads aloud, while Gohei, a thin man in a brown kimono and straw hat, looks over his shoulder toward the alley entrance, and a crowd of neighbors listens intently.

pages.text:
Okiku was waiting at her stall. She did not look surprised. She took the sheet from a customer, read it, and then stood very still. Her hands, usually quick and busy, rested on the counter.

Then she turned to the pot, cut a fresh slab of noodles into a bowl, and set it before the first person in line. "Eat," she said. "No coin. The truth is free."

The line grew. Haru stood at the back, watching. The broth was hot, the noodles slippery and strong. She tasted them. They were the best she had ever had, not because they were sweet, but because they were honest.

Kichi slurped loudly. "I was hungry," he said, as if that explained everything.

Okiku looked at Haru, and for a second, her eyes were soft. "You saved my name," she said quietly. "That is worth more than a year of coins."
pages.image: Okiku, an older woman with grey hair in a white towel and a faded pink quilted jacket, stands behind a wooden counter holding a bowl of noodles, while a line of neighbors in winter coats waits, and Haru in her rust-orange kimono watches from the back of the line.

pages.text:
The whisper died. The man who had claimed his cousin heard the rumor came by, bought a bowl, and ate quickly without meeting anyone’s eyes. He paid with a heavy coin and slipped away into the crowd.

Grandfather Tobei sat on the low step, his blue-grey kimono draped over his knees. He watched the street.

"A rumor," he said, "takes a day to travel a street. It takes a year to leave it." He tapped his walking stick on the stone. "But today is the first day of leaving. You pushed it out with your feet."

Haru felt a warmth in her chest that had nothing to do with the soup. She looked at her hands. They were clean, except for the faint ring of ink around her nails. She had done this. She had seen, and she had spoken, and the world had changed, just a little.

Kichi was already asking if there were more noodles.
pages.image: Grandfather Tobei, a thin old man with a white topknot and bushy eyebrows in a blue-grey kimono, sits on a wooden step tapping a walking stick, while Haru in her rust-orange kimono stands nearby looking at her ink-stained hands, and Kichi in his moss-green coat holds an empty bowl.

pages.text:
From across the alley, on the high step of the Turtle House, Jiro watched. He stood in his bright yellow silk kimono, his hands tucked into his sleeves. He did not look angry. He looked bored.

"Nobody reads true things," he called down, his voice smooth and cold. "They read exciting things. Foxes. Ghosts. Things that make their hearts beat fast."

He tilted his head. "In a month, you will see. The truth is quiet. Quiet doesn’t sell."

Haru held her booklet against her chest. The paper was cool against her stomach. She wanted to argue. She wanted to say that quiet things last longer. But the words stuck in her throat.

He might be right. The Turtle House sheets had sold out by noon, every single day. Haru looked at the empty space where the crowd had been. She did not believe Jiro. But she was not sure, either. And that doubt felt like a splinter under her skin.
pages.image: Jiro, a twelve-year-old boy in a bright yellow silk kimono with a black diamond pattern and a small topknot, stands on a high wooden step across a narrow alley, looking down with a bored expression, while Haru in her rust-orange kimono and indigo apron stands below holding a small booklet to her chest.
